steps.say: The commonest malignant brain tumour in adults is now defined as much by its genes as by its microscope appearance. Even without classic vessel growth or dead zones, certain chromosome changes alone earn the worst grade. Testing for those changes is therefore part of every diagnosis.
steps.tx: WHO 2021 defines **glioblastoma** (grade 4 brain cancer) as **IDH-wildtype** (no IDH mutation) diffuse astrocytic glioma with **microvascular proliferation** (abnormal vessel growth) or necrosis, or with TERT, EGFR or chromosome **7 and 10** (seven and ten) alterations even without those histology features. Molecular testing for **TERT** (telomere gene) and chromosome 7 gain with 10 loss is therefore mandatory at diagnosis.

steps.say: The scan of this tumour is dramatic: an irregular bright ring around a dead centre, swelling all around, and fingers reaching across the bridge between hemispheres. That butterfly spread across the middle separates it from lymphoma, which enhances evenly.
steps.tx: MRI shows an irregular **ring enhancement** (bright rim around dead centre) in a frontal or temporal mass with central necrosis, surrounding oedema and **butterfly glioma** (both-hemisphere spread) crossing the **corpus callosum** (hemisphere bridge). This ragged ring with necrosis separates glioblastoma from the homogeneous enhancement of primary brain lymphoma on the same scan.

vis.alt: Axial T1 post-contrast MRI of brain showing a large, irregularly enhancing glioblastoma with central necrosis, surrounding vasogenic oedema, and crossing the corpus callosum as a butterfly lesion.
vis.caption: Butterfly glioblastoma with ring enhancement, necrosis and callosal spread. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Surgeons remove as much as safely possible, using glowing dye and wake-up mapping near speech areas. Aggressive but careful removal extends life, and the tissue also reveals the markers that guide drug treatment. Maximal does not mean reckless near eloquent brain.
steps.tx: **Maximal safe resection** (largest careful removal) with **5-ALA fluorescence** (glow dye marking tumour) and awake mapping for eloquent lesions extends survival. Surgery also provides tissue for **MGMT methylation** (chemo-sensitivity marker) and NGS profiling that direct chemoradiation, so the operation both debulks and diagnoses for the oncologist.

vis.alt: Illustration of an awake craniotomy showing an awake patient, brain mapping with electrical stimulation, and neuronavigation.
vis.caption: Awake craniotomy with mapping for maximal safe resection near eloquence. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: After surgery, the standard recipe combines six weeks of radiation with daily chemo pills, then six monthly cycles of higher-dose pills. The doses and days are fixed by trial, and patients need blood-count checks throughout. This combined recipe added months of life over radiation alone.
steps.tx: The **Stupp protocol** (combined radio-chemo standard) gives **60 Gy** (sixty gray) in **30 fractions** (thirty sittings) with concurrent **temozolomide** (daily chemo pill) **75 mg** (seventy five milligrams) per sq m daily, then **6 cycles** (six rounds) of adjuvant temozolomide **150 to 200 mg** (one hundred fifty to two hundred milligrams) per sq m on days **1 to 5** (one to five) every **28 days** (twenty eight days).

vis.alt: Glioblastoma versus meningioma with Stupp protocol and surgical adjuncts.
vis.caption: Glioblastoma versus meningioma with the Stupp protocol and surgical adjuncts. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A chemical tag on the tumour's repair gene predicts who gains most from the chemo pills. Methylated tumours respond well, so even older patients get combined treatment. Unmethylated tumours in frail patients may receive radiation alone, sparing them pointless toxicity.
steps.tx: **MGMT methylation** (repair-gene silencing tag) predicts **temozolomide benefit** (chemo pill gain) and longer survival, so methylated **elderly glioblastoma** (older-patient tumour) cases get combined treatment. Unmethylated frail patients may receive radiotherapy alone, since the chemo adds toxicity without meaningful gain when the repair gene stays active.

steps.say: Fit young patients are not the only ones who can be treated. Shorter radiation over three weeks with the same chemo pills helps older or weaker patients live longer. The lower total dose keeps the burden tolerable while preserving the survival gain.
steps.tx: Elderly or poor-performance patients receive **hypofractionated radiotherapy** (shorter larger-dose radiation) of **40 Gy** (forty gray) in **15 fractions** (fifteen sittings) with temozolomide per the **Perry regimen** (elderly combined schedule). This balances survival against treatment burden, offering combined therapy even when the full six-week course would overwhelm.

steps.say: Newer options add modest gains or control swelling without extending life. A cap-like device worn on the scalp adds survival months, while an antibody calms swelling and radiation damage. When the tumour returns, an older nitrosourea drug remains the standard next step.
steps.tx: **Tumour-treating fields** (alternating electric-field cap) add survival in newly diagnosed disease per **EF-14** (device trial), while **bevacizumab** (vessel antibody) controls oedema and radiation necrosis without extending survival. **Lomustine** (nitrosourea chemo) is the standard recurrence chemotherapy when glioblastoma returns after Stupp treatment.

steps.say: The first scan after chemoradiation often looks worse even when treatment is working. Swelling and contrast uptake within three months usually mean inflammation, not regrowth. Special blood-flow and chemical scans tell true growth apart before anyone changes therapy.
steps.tx: **Pseudoprogression** (false early worsening) within **3 months** (three months) of chemoradiation mimics recurrence on MRI. **Perfusion MRI** (blood-flow scan) rCBV plus **MR spectroscopy** (chemical-peak scan) choline peaks separate it from true progression, so changing therapy waits for these advanced scans rather than reacting to the first alarming image.
